newsitem.title: BRAZIL: 'Great Train' robber Biggs thinks he's a lucky man.
newsitem.headline: 'Great Train' robber Biggs thinks he's a lucky man.

text.p: Ronnie Biggs, Britain's most famous fugitive who fled to Rio de Janeiro 27 years ago after taking part in a legendary heist known as the "Great Train Robbery", believes luck is on his side and doubts whether Brazil will extradite him after so many years.

A 1995 extradition treaty between Britain and Brazil is expected to be finally ratified by Britain in August, which increases the likelyhood of Biggs being forced to return to a British jail to serve the best part of his 30-year prison sentence.

"I have infinite faith that I won't go to jail," Biggs told Reuters on Wednesday during an interview at his home overlooking Rio. "I have been lucky until today and I hope I will continue to be lucky. In Brazil, everything is forgiven and forgotten after 20 years."

Biggs was part of a gang which in 1963 stole 2.6 million pounds - the equivalent of $50 million at today's values - from a Royal Mail train after fixing the track's signals and separating the sections of the train.
The robbers were eventually captured, but Biggs managed to jump the walls of a London jail and escape in 1965 after serving only 15 months of his jail term.

After having plastic surgery to change his appearance and hiding out in Australia under an assumed name, he settled in Brazil, a popular haven for international fugitives because of its lack of extradition laws.

His safety was further guaranteed when his son Michael was born because under Brazilian law Biggs could not be touched as long as he had a dependent. His son, who will turn 23 next month, is now legally independent.

However, the prospect of returning to jail after so many years of evading the authorities successfully does not seem to perturb the ageing thief who will turn 68 on August 8, the 34th anniversary of the "Great Train Robbery".

"It doesn't frighten me. I've lived with it too long to still worry about it," Biggs said as he petted his two-year-old Rottweiler, Blitz. "I'll just continue living the way I always have. I'm not going to run or do anything like that, but I will fight extradition in the courts."
Biggs, who has led a crime-free life since arriving in Brazil, has hired Brazilian and British lawyers to work on his case.

He has infuriated the authorities over the years by flaunting his freedom, appearing on television to promote his autobiography and living in an apartment with a giant Union Jack flag signed by his many visitors.

Only recently, one of Rio de Janeiro's many samba schools asked Biggs whether he would like to parade in next year's carnival to illustrate the school's parade theme "Hands up, this is an assault", but Biggs has rejected the offer.

"It's a negative subject and carnival is all about having fun. There are happier themes that I would like to be associated with like freedom, liberty," said Biggs, who does not regret the robbery as such.
